prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice atomic clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on this shortlist where a single, identifiable idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition so that many atoms can be interrogated in a Lamb-Dicke confined lattice) was turned into a measurement capability that is now reproduced and exceeded by independent laboratories. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, centimetre-scale tests of the gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter, and the pending redefinition of the second all follow directly. The attribution is the cleanest on the list: a two-person prize with Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to record accuracy and stability and extending them to many-body, spin-squeezed and cavity-enhanced regimes. The seven rankings (two first places, three top-three, all seven ranking members) show that this is also the candidate least dependent on one member's subfield. From my own atomic-structure perspective, the physics of magic wavelengths, polarisabilities and blackbody and other clock-transition shifts is well understood, so I can judge the maturity claim with some confidence. It also fills a clear gap: the comb (2005) and ion-trap quantum control and clocks (2012) were recognised, but the neutral-atom optical clock that now defines the state of the art was not.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision measurement with atoms and lasers has been recognised repeatedly (2005, 2012, and ultrafast optics in 2018 and 2023), so a committee could see this as a fourth return to AMO within about two decades and prefer a different field. A second concern is credit breadth: ion clocks (NIST, PTB), the Paris and JILA/NIST lattice groups, and theory work on magic wavelengths and systematic shifts all contributed, and a two-name prize leaves them out. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some colleagues may argue that the full impact is still to be demonstrated, although I regard the demonstrated accuracy and the many independent confirmations as sufficient.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock sixth and says that Ye already shared the 2005 prize for frequency-comb work, which may affect the committee's view of recognising him again.
responses.response: I think this premise is factually wrong and should be corrected before it influences the discussion. The 2005 prize for the frequency comb went to Hall and Hansch; Ye was a leading figure in Hall's group but was not a laureate, so there is no repeat-recognition issue for him. Even if there were, the lattice clock is a distinct achievement from comb metrology: it rests on Katori's magic-wavelength idea and on a separate decade of work on coherence and systematics. I do agree with Pearce that the thematic proximity to 2005 and 2012 is a legitimate concern, but it argues for asking whether the new achievement is distinct in concept and impact, and I think it plainly is.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first and trapped-ion computation second, with the lattice clock fourth, and also notes that Ye shared the 2005 comb context.
responses.response: I take seriously the argument that circuit QED and the Cirac-Zoller proposals have large influence on quantum technology, but I weigh them below the clock for reasons of timing and attribution. The 2022 prize on entanglement and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits both sit very close to B008, and for B029 the experimental credit is unclear because Wineland has already been honoured and Monroe and others are also central. I would also not equate quantum-computing impact with scientific merit; the clock is a finished, reproduced achievement with a concrete record. I would, however, accept B029 or B008 as a worthy later prize and do not dismiss them.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active matter first and the clock fifth, describing the clock as mostly experimental metrology rather than a conceptual advance, while still crediting its large impact.
responses.response: I disagree with the framing that the clock is only metrology. Magic-wavelength trapping is a conceptual step in the control of atomic internal and motional states, and the ensuing many-body physics (collisional shifts, spin squeezing, interaction-driven effects in lattice clocks) now supplies a direct window on quantum many-body behaviour. That said, I agree with Mehlig on the scientific depth and maturity of active matter, which has three decades of theory and quantitative experimental tests; my own concern there is that I cannot assess the attribution, since Tu is missing from the credited set despite his role in the Toner-Tu theory, and I would want to hear how the committee weighs that omission.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation first, arguing that the experimental discovery completed the Standard Model and has never been recognised, but concedes that credit assignment among the collaboration is the hardest part.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation is of the highest scientific significance and that it is overdue in principle, and I ranked it seventh only because of the attribution problem, not merit. Founding proposers and detector leaders are a proxy for, not an identification of, the people who made the discovery, and with two experiments the three-person limit forces an essentially arbitrary choice. Unless Danielsson or others can propose an allocation that the committee finds defensible, I think a prize on a candidate with two-name credit that matches the actual intellectual origin is the safer and more principled outcome.

responses.point: Olsson ranks solid-state femtosecond lasers first and the lattice clock fourth, citing the lattice clock's pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait slightly.
responses.response: I do not think the pending redefinition is a reason to wait; the Nobel Prize recognises the discovery, not the outcome of a metrological decision, and the clock accuracy has already been reproduced in several independent laboratories. On B004 I note a connection: Keller's group at ETH has been a collaborator of mine, so I would prefer not to be the one to weigh its merits, and I would add that ultrafast optics was recognised in 2018 and 2023, which in my view reduces the urgency compared with the clock.

uncertainties: How much weight colleagues will put on recent atomic and quantum-optics prizes (2005, 2012, 2022, 2023) when comparing the clock with a condensed-matter or particle-physics alternative.
Whether the omission of other lattice-clock and ion-clock contributors (for example Lemonde, Hinkley, Ludlow, Derevianko) from a two-person credit is judged acceptable.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding the clock.

For B018, whether the unsettled mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is too early; for B042, whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu makes a three-name credit unfair.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund group, and papers with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, so I should disclose a connection if B004 (Keller) is discussed in depth and would consider recusal on that ballot. I also work in atomic theory in the same broad field as B037, B016 and B029, but no specific connection to Katori or Ye is documented in the provided profile, and no specific conflict is apparent for B037.
